text:
Probably yes, as long as closing costs stay under roughly $10k.

Assuming a 30-year term on both, the payment drops from about $2,528 to $2,373, saving roughly $155/month. Closing costs typically run 2-3% of the loan, so $8k-$12k. That puts breakeven at about 52 months at $8k or 77 months at $12k. Over 10 years you'd save about $18,600 in payments, so net of costs you come out ahead by roughly $6,500-$10,500, and a bit more because you also build equity faster at the lower rate.

Several things can change that:

- **Loan age:** If you're several years into the current loan, a fresh 30-year term lowers the payment partly by stretching it out. Compare against your remaining term, or keep paying the old payment amount ($2,528) on the new loan to shorten it and save much more interest.
- **Closing costs:** Get actual Loan Estimates from 2-3 lenders. If costs are above about $12k, the case gets thin. Lender credits or no-closing-cost options trade a slightly higher rate for no upfront cost, which can make sense if you're unsure about the 10 years.
- **Rolling costs into the loan:** This works, but you pay interest on them and breakeven moves out.
- **Waiting:** If rates keep falling, you could refinance again, but that means paying closing costs twice. Don't wait on a guess when the math already works.

If you share your remaining term and a real closing cost quote, I can run the exact breakeven.
